Yes, radios were used in the trenches during World War I, though their use evolved significantly over the course of the war. [d1] One of the earliest radios deployed in the trenches was the 50-watt BF Trench Set, which "went into action in the Battle of Loos in September 1915 and in the first Battle of the Somme on July 1st 1916," with approximately 1,200 manufactured. [d3] The National Archives confirms that telecommunications apparatus adapted for British soldiers in the trenches included "modified cavalry field radios to field communication devices for gun spotters." [d5] According to Britannica, prewar radio sets were initially "too heavy and bulky to be taken into the trenches," but radio engineers "soon developed smaller and more portable sets powered by storage batteries," and radio equipment eventually came to be issued to the headquarters of all units, including battalions. [d4] The Canadian War Museum similarly notes that while early wireless sets were "bulky and fragile, with relatively short ranges," later more robust wireless sets were used by observers to direct artillery fire. [d6] The U.S. Army history source notes that despite limitations—including interference and weight of up to 500 pounds for some sets—the Signal Corps developed approximately twenty-five different radio types by the war's end, though "radio carried little of the war's communications load" compared to wire systems. [d2] Overall, as Scientific American reported, "the telephone, telegraph and the appearance of effective wireless radio sets were replacing older communication methods," with radios becoming increasingly important as the war progressed.
